item.title: Disseminated Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Disease in NEMO and Iκbα Defects
item.description:
Abstract
Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacterial disease is a severe complication of NEMO (IKBKG) and IκBα (NFKBIA) defects. It may present in adulthood, and diagnosis was often delayed. Despite intensive multidrug therapy and adjunctive IFN-γ, treatment responses were frequently inadequate. Hematopoietic cell transplantation may offer immune reconstitution but carries risks.

item.title: Holistic Composite Endpoints With Strategic Analyses: Toward More Informed Clinical Decision-Making for Gram-Negative Bacterial Bloodstream Infections
item.description: Increasing resistance in common bacterial pathogens to available antibiotic treatment options is a slow-moving, ongoing, unrelenting global health crisis that impacts all fields of medicine. In gram-negative bacteria, 2 mechanisms of resistance are increasingly important and prevalent worldwide. First, enzymatically mediated resistance due to metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs) is on the rise. Of these, the New Delhi MBL (NDM) is the most important family. Recent epidemiologic trends suggest that NDM has now replaced the serine carbapenemase family of Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase as the most common cause of enzymatic carbapenem resistance in Enterobacterales in the United States [1, 2]. A second concern involves Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae strains with insert mutations in the gene encoding penicillin-binding protein 3 (PBP3) rendering them less susceptible to β-lactam antibiotics—including cefiderocol—that bind primarily to PBP3 [3]. In addition to antibiotic stewardship and infection prevention measures that decrease the spread of resistance, novel antibiotics and adjunctive therapies, such as bacteriophages and monoclonals, are needed to treat patients infected with these resistant bacteria. Cefiderocol was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2019, with promisingly broad in vitro activity that includes the highest priority gram-negative bacteria. Seven years later, the question of how best to use this agent is not yet resolved. In this issue of Clinical Infectious Diseases, Hardy et al report a secondary analysis of the GAME CHANGER trial; an open-label randomized trial, in which cefiderocol was noninferior to standard of care for the primary endpoint of 14-day mortality in patients with gram-negative nosocomial bloodstream infection [4]. In the carbapenem-resistant subset, 14-day mortality was 14% (9/64) in the cefiderocol arm versus 10% (6/63) in the standard-of-care arm, with a notable difference in mortality (5/16 vs 0/11) in patients infected with MBL producers [4, 5]. While limited by small numbers, this suggests caution when considering the use of cefiderocol in patients infected with MBL producers. This effect appears primarily driven by bacteria that produce enzymes in the NDM family, which more effectively hydrolyze cefiderocol when compared to other MBL enzymes [5].
